section.heading: 3. Differentiation
Introduction
section.paragraph: T his chapter gives several rules that will greatly simplify the task of finding the derivative of a function, thus enabling us to study how fast one quantity is changing with respect to another in many real-world situations. For example, we will be able to find how fast the population of an endangered species of whales grows after certain conservation measures have been implemented, how fast an economy’s consumer price index (CPI) is changing at any time, and how fast the time taken to learn the items on a list changes with respect to the length of a list. We also see how these rules of differentiation facilitate the study of the rate of change of economic quantities—that is, the study of marginal analysis. Finally, we introduce the notion of the differential of a function. Differentials are used to approximate the change in one quantity due to a small change in a related quantity.

section.heading: 3.1. Basic Rules of Differentiation
Four Basic Rules
section.paragraph: The method used in Chapter 2 for computing the derivative of a function is based on a faithful interpretation of the definition of the derivative as the limit of a quotient. To find the rule for the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of a function $$f$$ , we first computed the difference quotient
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
and then evaluated its limit as $$h$$ approached zero. As you have probably observed, this method is tedious even for relatively simple functions.
The main purpose of this chapter is to derive certain rules that will simplify the process of finding the derivative of a function. We will use the notation
$$\frac{d}{dx}\lbrack f(x)\rbrack { \text{Read “} d,dx \text{of} f \text{of} x \text{”} }$$
to mean “the derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ at $$x$$ .”

note.source_type: Rule 1: Derivative of a Constant
note.title: Rule 1: Derivative of a Constant
note.heading: Rule 1: Derivative of a Constant
note.paragraph: $$\frac{d}{dx}(c) = 0 {(c, \text{a constant} )}$$

section.paragraph: The derivative of a constant function is equal to zero.

We can see this from a geometric viewpoint by recalling that the graph of a constant function is a straight line parallel to the $$x$$ -axis (Figure 1). Since the tangent line to a straight line at any point on the line coincides with the straight line itself, its slope [as given by the derivative of $$f(x) = c$$ ] must be zero. We can also use the definition of the derivative to prove this result by computing

$$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{c - c}{h}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}0 = 0} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Let’s verify the Power Rule for the special case $$n = 2$$ . If $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , then

as we set out to show.
The Power Rule for the general case is not easy to prove, and its proof will be omitted. However, you will be asked to prove the rule for the special case $$n = 3$$ in Exercise 78.

section.paragraph: The derivative of the sum (difference) of two differentiable functions is equal to the sum (difference) of their derivatives.
This result may be extended to the sum and difference of any finite number of differentiable functions. Let’s verify the rule for a sum of two functions.
If $$s(x) = f(x) + g(x)$$ , then

$$\begin{array}{l} {s^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{s(x + h) - s(x)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{s^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left\lbrack f(x + h) + g(x + h) \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack f(x) + g(x) \right\rbrack}{h}} \\ {\phantom{s^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left\lbrack f(x + h) - f(x) \right\rbrack + \left\lbrack g(x + h) - g(x) \right\rbrack}{h}} \\ {\phantom{s^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{s^{\prime}(x)} = f^{\prime}(x) + g^{\prime}(x)} \end{array}$$

note.title: Applied Example 8. Altitude of a Rocket
note.heading: Applied Example 8. Altitude of a Rocket
note.paragraph: An experimental rocket lifts off vertically. Its altitude (in feet) $$t$$ seconds into flight is given by

list.item: Find an expression $$v$$ for the rocket’s velocity at any time $$t$$ .
Compute the rocket’s velocity when $$t = 0,30,50,64, \text{and} 70$$ . Interpret your results.
Using the results from the solution to part (b) and the observation that at the highest point in its trajectory the rocket’s velocity is zero, find the maximum altitude attained by the rocket.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The rocket’s velocity at any time $$t$$ is given by $$v = f^{\prime}(t) = - 3t^{2} + 192t$$

The rocket’s velocity when $$t = 0,30,50,64, \text{and} 70$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{rll} {f^{\prime}(0)} & = & {- 3{(0)}^{2} + 192(0) = 0} \\ {f^{\prime}(30)} & = & {- 3(30)^{2} + 192(30) = 3060} \\ {f^{\prime}(50)} & = & {- 3{(50)}^{2} + 192(50) = 2100} \\ {f^{\prime}(64)} & = & {- 3{(64)}^{2} + 192(64) = 0} \\ {f^{\prime}(70)} & = & {- 3(70)^{2} + 192(70) = - 1260} \end{array}$$ or $$0$$ , $$3060$$ , $$2100$$ , $$0$$ , and $$- 1260$$ feet per second $$\left( {ft} \slash \sec \right)$$ . Thus, the rocket has an initial velocity of $$0{ft} \slash \sec$$ at $$t = 0$$ and accelerates to a velocity of $$3060{ft} \slash \sec$$ at $$t = 30$$ . Fifty seconds into the flight, the rocket’s velocity is $$2100{ft} \slash \sec$$ , which is less than the velocity at $$t = 30$$ . This means that the rocket begins to decelerate after an initial period of acceleration. (Later on, we will learn how to determine the rocket’s maximum velocity.) The deceleration continues: The velocity is $$0{ft} \slash \sec$$ at $$t = 64$$ and $$- 1260{ft} \slash \sec$$ when $$t = 70$$ . This result tells us that $$70$$ seconds into flight, the rocket is heading back to the earth with a speed of $$1260{ft} \slash \sec$$ .

The results of part (b) show that the rocket’s velocity is zero when $$t = 64$$ . At this instant, the rocket’s maximum altitude is $$\begin{array}{l} {s = f(64) = - (64)^{3} + 96{(64)}^{2} + 5} \\ {\phantom{s} = 131,077} \end{array}$$ or $$131,077$$ feet. note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: You may have observed that the domain of the function $$f$$ in Example 8 is restricted, for practical reasons, to the interval $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ . Since the definition of the derivative of a function $$f$$ at a number $$a$$ requires that $$f$$ be defined in an open interval containing $$a$$ , the derivative of $$f$$ is not, strictly speaking, defined at $$0$$ . But notice that the function $$f$$ can, in fact, be defined for all values of $$t$$ , and hence it makes sense to calculate $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ . You will encounter situations such as this throughout the book, especially in exercises pertaining to real-world applications. The nature of the functions appearing in these applications obviates the necessity to consider “one-sided” derivatives.

section.heading: 3.2. The Product and Quotient Rules
section.paragraph: In this section, we study two more rules of differentiation: the Product Rule and the Quotient Rule.
section.heading: The Product Rule
section.paragraph: The derivative of the product of two differentiable functions is given by the following rule:

note.source_type: Rule 5: The Product Rule
note.title: Rule 5: The Product Rule
note.heading: Rule 5: The Product Rule
note.paragraph: $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack = f(x)g^{\prime}(x) + g(x)f^{\prime}(x)$$

section.paragraph: The derivative of the product of two functions is the first function times the derivative of the second plus the second function times the derivative of the first.
The Product Rule may be extended to the case involving the product of any finite number of functions (see Exercise 73). We prove the Product Rule at the end of this section.
The derivative of the product of two functions is not given by the product of the derivatives of the functions; that is, in general
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack \neq f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x)$$
For example, if $$f(x) = x$$ and $$g(x) = 2x^{2}$$ . Then
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack x(2x^{2})\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(2x^{3}) = 6x^{2}$$
On the other hand, $$f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x) = (1)(4x) = 4x$$ . So
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack \neq f^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(x)$$

section.heading: The Quotient Rule
section.paragraph: The derivative of the quotient of two differentiable functions is given by the following rule:

note.source_type: Rule 6: The Quotient Rule
note.title: Rule 6: The Quotient Rule
note.heading: Rule 6: The Quotient Rule
note.paragraph: $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack = \frac{g(x)f^{\prime}(x) - f(x)g^{\prime}(x)}{\left\lbrack g(x) \right\rbrack^{2}} (g(x) \neq 0)$$

section.paragraph: As an aid to remembering this expression, observe that it has the following form:

$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack = \frac{({Denominator})\left( \begin{array}{l} {Derivative of} \\ {numerator} \end{array} \right) - ({Numerator})\left( \begin{array}{l} {Derivative of} \\ {denominator} \end{array} \right)}{({Square of denominator})}$$
For a proof of the Quotient Rule, see Exercise 74.
The derivative of a quotient is not equal to the quotient of the derivatives; that is,
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack \neq \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$$
For example, if $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ , then
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right\rbrack = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{x^{3}}{x^{2}} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x) = 1$$
which is not equal to
$$\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{3})}{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{2})} = \frac{3x^{2}}{2x} = \frac{3}{2}x$$

note.paragraph: When organic waste is dumped into a pond, the oxidation process that takes place reduces the pond’s oxygen content. However, given time, nature will restore the oxygen content to its natural level. Suppose the oxygen content $$t$$ days after organic waste has been dumped into the pond is given by

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The rate of change of the pond’s oxygen level at any time $$t$$ is given by the derivative of the function $$f$$ . Thus, the required expression is $$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(t) = 100\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack \frac{t^{2} + 10t + 100}{t^{2} + 20t + 100} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{(t^{2} + 20t + 100)\frac{d}{dt}(t^{2} + 10t + 100) - (t^{2} + 10t + 100)\frac{d}{dt}(t^{2} + 20t + 100)}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)(2t + 10) - \left( t^{2} + 10t + 100 \right)(2t + 20)}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{2t^{3} + 10t^{2} + 40t^{2} + 200t + 200t + 1000 - 2t^{3} - 20t^{2} - 20t^{2} - 200t - 200t - 2000}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10t^{2} - 1000}{\left( t^{2} + 20t + 100 \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack \text{Combine like terms in the numerator.} } \end{array}$$ Algebra See Example 2.

The rate at which the pond’s oxygen content is changing $$1$$ day after the organic waste has been dumped is given by $$f^{\prime}(1) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10 - 1000}{(1 + 20 + 100)^{2}} \right\rbrack \approx - 6.76$$ That is, it is dropping at the rate of $$6.8\%$$ per day. After $$10$$ days, the rate is $$f^{\prime}(10) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10(10)^{2} - 1000}{{(10^{2} + 20(10) + 100)}^{2}} \right\rbrack = 0$$ That is, it is neither increasing nor decreasing. After $$20$$ days, the rate is $$f^{\prime}(20) = 100\left\lbrack \frac{10(20)^{2} - 1000}{{(20^{2} + 20(20) + 100)}^{2}} \right\rbrack \approx 0.37$$ That is, the oxygen content is increasing at the rate of $$0.37\%$$ per day, and the restoration process has indeed begun.

section.heading: Verification of the Product Rule
section.paragraph: We will now verify the Product Rule. If $$p(x) = f(x)g(x)$$ , then
$$p^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{p(x + h) - p(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h)g(x + h) - f(x)g(x)}{h}$$
By adding $$- f(x + h)g(x) + f(x + h)g(x)$$ (which is zero!) to the numerator and factoring, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {p^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h)\left\lbrack g(x + h) - g(x) \right\rbrack + g(x)\left\lbrack f(x + h) - f(x) \right\rbrack}{h}} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left\{ {f(x + h)\left\lbrack \frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} \right\rbrack + g(x)\left\lbrack \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \right\rbrack} \right\}} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h)\left\lbrack \frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} \right\rbrack + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}g(x)\left\lbrack \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \right\rbrack { \text{By Property} 3 \text{of limits} }} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h) \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h} + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}g(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} { \text{By Property} 4 \text{of limits} }} \\ {\phantom{p^{\prime}(x)} = f(x)g^{\prime}(x) + g(x)f^{\prime}(x)} \end{array}$$
Observe that in the last link in the chain of equalities, we have used the fact that $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}f(x + h) = f(x)$$ because $$f$$ is continuous at $$x$$ .

section.heading: 3.4. Marginal Functions in Economics
section.paragraph: Marginal analysis is the study of the rate of change of economic quantities. For example, an economist is not merely concerned with the value of an economy’s gross domestic product (GDP) at a given time but is equally concerned with the rate at which it is growing or declining. In the same vein, a manufacturer is not only interested in the total cost corresponding to a certain level of production of a commodity but also is interested in the rate of change of the total cost with respect to the level of production, and so on. Let’s begin with an example to explain the meaning of the adjective marginal, as used by economists.

Find the rate of change of the total cost function with respect to $$x$$ when $$x = 250$$ .

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The actual cost incurred in producing the 251st refrigerator is the difference between the total cost incurred in producing the first $$251$$ refrigerators and the total cost of producing the first $$250$$ refrigerators: $$\begin{array}{l} {C(251) - C(250) = {\lbrack{8000 + 200(251) - 0.2(251)^{2}}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{8000 + 200(250) - 0.2(250)^{2}}\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{C(251) - C(250)}{= 45,599.8 - 45,500}} \\ {\phantom{C(251) - C(250)} = 99.8} \end{array}$$ or $$\$ 99.80$$ .

The rate of change of the total cost function $$C$$ with respect to $$x$$ is given by the derivative of $$C$$ —that is, $$C^{\prime}(x) = 200 - 0.4x$$ . Thus, when the level of production is $$250$$ refrigerators, the rate of change of the total cost with respect to $$x$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {C^{\prime}(250) = 200 - 0.4(250)} \\ {\phantom{C^{\prime}(250)} = 100} \end{array}$$ or $$\$ 100$$ .

From the solution to part (a), we know that the actual cost for producing the 251st refrigerator is $$\$ 99.80$$ . This answer is very closely approximated by the answer to part (b), $$\$ 100$$ . To see why this is so, observe that the difference $$C(251) - C(250)$$ may be written in the form $$\frac{C(251) - C(250)}{1} = \frac{C(250 + 1) - C(250)}{1} = \frac{C(250 + h) - C(250)}{h}$$ where $$h = 1$$ . In other words, the difference $$C(251) - C(250)$$ is precisely the average rate of change of the total cost function $$C$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {250,251} \right\rbrack$$ or, equivalently, the slope of the secant line through the points $$\left( {250,45,500} \right)$$ and $$\left( {251,45,599.8} \right)$$ . However, the number $$C^{\prime}(250) = 100$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of the total cost function $$C$$ at $$x = 250$$ or, equivalently, the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$C$$ at $$x = 250$$ . Now when $$h$$ is small, the average rate of change of the function $$C$$ is a good approximation to the instantaneous rate of change of the function $$C$$ , or, equivalently, the slope of the secant line through the points in question is a good approximation to the slope of the tangent line through the point in question. Therefore, we may expect $$\begin{array}{l} {C(251) - C(250) = \frac{C(251) - C(250)}{1} \approx \frac{C(250 + h) - C(250)}{h}(h \text{small} )} \\ {\phantom{C(251) - C(250)}{\approx \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{C(250 + h) - C(250)}{h} = C^{\prime}(250)}} \end{array}$$ which is precisely the case in this example.

section.paragraph: The actual cost incurred in producing an additional unit of a certain commodity given that a plant is already at a certain level of operation is called the marginal cost . Knowing this cost is very important to management. As we saw in Example 1, the marginal cost is approximated by the rate of change of the total cost function evaluated at the appropriate point. For this reason, economists have defined the marginal cost function to be the derivative of the corresponding total cost function. In other words, if $$C$$ is a total cost function, then the marginal cost function is defined to be its derivative $$C^{\prime}$$ . Thus, the adjective marginal is synonymous with derivative of.

section.heading: Elasticity of Demand
section.paragraph: Finally, let’s use the marginal concepts introduced in this section to derive an important criterion that economists use to analyze a demand function: elasticity of demand. This measurement enables a businessperson to see how a small percentage change in the price of a commodity affects the percentage change in the quantity demanded of the commodity.

In what follows, it will be convenient to write the demand function $$f$$ in the form $$x = f(p)$$ ; that is, we will think of the quantity demanded of a certain commodity as a function of its unit price. Since the quantity demanded of a commodity usually decreases as its unit price increases, the function $$f$$ is typically a decreasing function of $$p$$ (Figure 13).

section.paragraph: Since the rate of change of the demand function with respect to $$p$$ is $$f^{\prime}(p)$$ , we see that the relative rate of change of $$f$$ with respect to $$p$$ at $$p$$ is
$$\frac{f^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}$$
or
Next, we see that the relative rate of change of the price $$p$$ of the commodity is
$$\frac{\frac{d}{dp}(p)}{p} = \frac{1}{p}$$
or
Therefore,
$$\frac{ \text{Percentage rate of change of} f}{ \text{Percentage rate of change of} p} = \frac{\frac{100f^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}}{\frac{100}{p}} = \frac{pf^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}$$
Economists call the negative of this quantity the elasticity of demand.

note.heading: Elasticity of Demand
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a differentiable demand function defined by $$x = f(p)$$ , then the elasticity of demand at price $$p$$ is given by
$$E(p) = - \frac{pf^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}$$

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: It will be shown later (in Section 4.1) that if $$f$$ is decreasing on an interval, then $$f^{\prime}(p) < 0$$ for $$p$$ in that interval. In light of this, we see that since both $$p$$ and $$f(p)$$ are positive, the quantity $$\frac{pf^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}$$ is negative. Because economists would rather work with a positive value, the elasticity of demand $$E(p)$$ is defined to be the negative of this quantity.

section.paragraph: Economists often use the following terminology to describe demand in terms of elasticity.

note.source_type: Elasticity of Demand
note.title: Elasticity of Demand
note.heading: Elasticity of Demand
note.paragraph: The demand is said to be elastic if $$E(p) > 1$$ .
The demand is said to be unitary if $$E(p) = 1$$ .
The demand is said to be inelastic if $$E(p) < 1$$ .

section.paragraph: As an illustration, our computations in Example 8 revealed that demand for Acrosonic loudspeakers is elastic when $$p = 300$$ but inelastic when $$p = 100$$ . These computations confirm that when demand is elastic, a small percentage change in the unit price will result in a greater percentage change in the quantity demanded; and when demand is inelastic, a small percentage change in the unit price will cause a smaller percentage change in the quantity demanded. Finally, when demand is unitary, a small percentage change in the unit price will result in approximately the same percentage change in the quantity demanded.

We can describe the way revenue responds to changes in the unit price using the notion of elasticity. If the quantity demanded of a certain commodity is related to its unit price by the equation $$x = f(p)$$ , then the revenue realized through the sale of $$x$$ units of the commodity at a price of $$p$$ dollars each is
$$R(p) = px = pf(p)$$
The rate of change of the revenue with respect to the unit price $$p$$ is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {R^{\prime}(p) = f(p) + pf^{\prime}(p)} \\ {\phantom{R^{\prime}(p)}{= f(p)\left\lbrack 1 + \frac{pf^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{R^{\prime}(p)}{= f(p)\left\lbrack 1 - E(p) \right\rbrack}} \end{array}$$
Now, suppose demand is elastic when the unit price is set at $$a$$ dollars. Then $$E(a) > 1$$ , and so $$1 - E(a) < 0$$ . Since $$f(p)$$ is positive for all values of $$p$$ , we see that
$$R^{\prime}(a) = f(a)\left\lbrack 1 - E(a) \right\rbrack < 0$$

and so $$R(p)$$ is decreasing at $$p = a$$ . This implies that a small increase in the unit price when $$p = a$$ results in a decrease in the revenue, whereas a small decrease in the unit price will result in an increase in the revenue. Similarly, you can show that if the demand is inelastic when the unit price is set at $$a$$ dollars, then a small increase in the unit price will cause the revenue to increase, and a small decrease in the unit price will cause the revenue to decrease. Finally, if the demand is unitary when the unit price is set at $$a$$ dollars, then $$E(a) = 1$$ and $$R^{\prime}(a) = 0$$ . This implies that a small increase or decrease in the unit price will not result in a change in the revenue. The following statements summarize this discussion.

list.item: If the demand is elastic at $$p\left\lbrack E(p) > 1 \right\rbrack$$ , then a small increase in the unit price will cause the revenue to decrease, whereas a small decrease in the unit price will cause the revenue to increase.

If the demand is inelastic at $$p\left\lbrack E(p) < 1 \right\rbrack$$ , then a small increase in the unit price will cause the revenue to increase, and a small decrease in the unit price will cause the revenue to decrease.
If the demand is unitary at $$p\left\lbrack E(p) = 1 \right\rbrack$$ , then a small increase or decrease in the unit price will cause the revenue to stay about the same.

section.paragraph: The derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of a function $$f$$ is also a function. As such, the differentiability of $$f^{\prime}$$ may be considered. Thus, the function $$f^{\prime}$$ has a derivative $$f^{''}$$ at a point $$x$$ in the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ if the limit of the quotient
$$\frac{f^{\prime}(x + h) - f^{\prime}(x)}{h}$$
exists as $$h$$ approaches zero. In other words, it is the derivative of the first derivative.

The function $$f^{''}$$ obtained in this manner is called the second derivative of the function $$f$$ , just as the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of $$f$$ is often called the first derivative of $$f$$ . note.source_type: Applied Example 6. Output of a Country
note.title: Applied Example 6. Output of a Country
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Output of a Country
note.paragraph: The chief economist of a country estimates that the output of the country is given by $$Q = 10x^{3 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4}$$ , where $$x$$ is the amount of money spent on labor and $$y$$ is the amount spent on capital. Here, $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$Q$$ are measured in billions of dollars.

list.item: Find the output of the country if $$\$ 625$$ billion is spent on labor and $$\$ 81$$ billion is spent on capital.

Suppose that the output of the country is to be maintained at the level found in part (a). By how much should the amount spent on capital be changed if the amount spent on labor is to be increased by $$\$ 1$$ billion?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: Replacing $$x$$ and $$y$$ by $$625$$ and $$81$$ , respectively, in the expression for $$Q$$ , we see that the required output is $$Q = 10(625)^{3 \slash 4}(81)^{1 \slash 4} = 3750$$ or $$\$ 3750$$ billion.

We want to find the change in $$y$$ per unit change in $$x$$ when $$x = 625$$ and $$y = 81$$ given that $$10x^{3 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4} = 3750$$ . But as you saw in Section 3.4, this quantity is approximated by $$dy \slash dx$$ (evaluated at the specified values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ ). To find $$dy \slash dx$$ , we differentiate the equation $$10x^{3 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4} = 3750$$ or, equivalently, the equation $$x^{3 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4} = 375$$ implicitly. Thus, $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4})} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(375)} \\ {\frac{3}{4}x^{- 1 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4} + x^{3 \slash 4}\left( \frac{1}{4}y^{- 3 \slash 4}\frac{dy}{dx} \right)} & = & 0 \\ {\frac{1}{4}x^{3 \slash 4}y^{- 3 \slash 4}\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & {- \frac{3}{4}x^{- 1 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4}} \end{array}$$ or $$\frac{dy}{dx} = (4x^{- 3 \slash 4}y^{3 \slash 4})\left( - \frac{3}{4}x^{- 1 \slash 4}y^{1 \slash 4} \right) = - 3x^{- 1}y = - 3\left( \frac{y}{x} \right)$$ Therefore, when $$x = 625$$ and $$y = 81$$ , we find $$\frac{dy}{dx} = - 3\left( \frac{81}{625} \right) = - 0.3888$$ So to keep the output at the constant level of $$\$ 3750$$ billion, the amount spent on capital should decrease by $$\$ 0.3888$$ billion if the amount spent on labor were to be increased by $$\$ 1$$ billion.

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: The negative of $$dy \slash dx$$ found in Example 6 is called the marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS). In general, the MRTS measures the rate at which a producer is technically able to reduce one input (capital) for a unit increase of another input (labor) while maintaining a constant level of output. Thus, the MRTS for the country in Example 6 is $$\$ 0.3888$$ billion per $$\$ 1$$ billion.

section.heading: Related Rates
section.paragraph: Implicit differentiation is a useful technique for solving a class of problems known as related-rates problems. The following is a typical related-rates problem: Suppose $$x$$ and $$y$$ are two quantities that depend on a third quantity $$t$$ and we know the relationship between $$x$$ and $$y$$ in the form of an equation. Can we find a relationship between $$dx \slash dt$$ and $$dy \slash dt$$ ? In particular, if we know one of the rates of change at a specific value of $$t$$ —say, $$dx \slash dt$$ —can we find the other rate, $$dy \slash dt$$ , at that value of $$t$$ ?

section.heading: 3.7. Differentials
section.paragraph: The Millers are planning to buy a house in the near future and estimate that they will need a $$30$$ -year fixed-rate mortgage of $$\$ 240,000$$ . If the interest rate increases from the present rate of $$5\%$$ per year to $$5.4\%$$ per year between now and the time the Millers decide to secure the loan, approximately how much more per month will their mortgage be? (You will be asked to answer this question in Exercise 46.)

Questions such as this, in which one wishes to estimate the change in the dependent variable (monthly mortgage payment) corresponding to a small change in the independent variable (interest rate per year), occur in many real-life applications. For example:

list.item: An economist would like to know how a small increase in a country’s capital expenditure will affect the country’s gross domestic output.
A sociologist would like to know how a small increase in the amount of capital investment in a housing project will affect the crime rate.
A businesswoman would like to know how raising a product’s unit price by a small amount will affect her profit.
A bacteriologist would like to know how a small increase in the amount of a bactericide will affect a population of bacteria.

section.paragraph: To calculate these changes and estimate their effects, we use the differential of a function, a concept that will be introduced shortly.
section.heading: Increments
section.paragraph: Let $$x$$ denote a variable quantity and suppose $$x$$ changes from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ . This change in $$x$$ is called the increment in $$\mathbf{x}$$ and is denoted by the symbol $$\Delta x$$ (read “delta $$x$$ ”). Thus,
$$\Delta x = x_{2} - x_{1} {{Final value} - {initial value}}$$

section.paragraph: Observe that near the point of tangency $$P$$ , the tangent line $$T$$ is close to the graph of $$f$$ . Therefore, if $$\Delta x$$ is small, then $$dy$$ is a good approximation of $$\Delta y$$ . We can find an expression for $$dy$$ as follows. Notice that the slope of $$T$$ is given by
$$\frac{dy}{\Delta x} {{Rise} \div {run}}$$
However, the slope of $$T$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . Therefore, we have
$$\frac{dy}{\Delta x} = f^{\prime}(x)$$
or $$dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x$$ . Thus, we have the approximation
$$\Delta y \approx dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x$$
in terms of the derivative of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . The quantity $$dy$$ is called the differential of $$y$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe how much easier it is to find an approximation to the exact change in a function with the help of the differential, rather than calculating the exact change in the function itself. In the following examples, we take advantage of this fact.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Approximate the value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ using differentials. Verify your result using the $$\boxed{\sqrt{}}$$ key on your calculator.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Since we want to compute the square root of a number, let’s consider the function $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . Since $$25$$ is the number nearest $$26.5$$ whose square root is readily recognized, let’s take $$x = 25$$ . We want to know the change in $$y$$ , $$\Delta y$$ , as $$x$$ changes from $$x = 25$$ to $$x = 26.5$$ , an increase of $$\Delta x = 1.5$$ units. Using Equation (12), we find

$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta y \approx dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x} \\ {\phantom{\Delta y \approx dy} = \left( \left. \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \right|_{x = 25} \right) \cdot (1.5) = \left( \frac{1}{10} \right)(1.5) = 0.15} \end{array}$$
The exact value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ , rounded off to five decimal places, is $$5.14782$$ . Thus, the error incurred in the approximation is $$0.00218$$ .

Recent observations, including those of Voyager I and II, showed that Neptune’s ring system is considerably more complex than had been believed. For one thing, it is made up of a large number of distinguishable rings rather than one continuous great ring as was previously thought (Figure 23b). The outermost ring, 1989N1R, has an inner radius of approximately $$62,900$$ kilometers (measured from the center of the planet) and a radial width of approximately $$50$$ kilometers. Using these data, estimate the area of the ring.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: Since the area of a circle of radius $$x$$ is $$A = f(x) = \pi x^{2}$$ , we find $$\begin{array}{l} {\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2} = f(R) - f(r)} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} = \Delta A \begin{array}{l} { \text{Remember,} \Delta A = \text{change in} f \text{when} x} \\ { \text{changes from} x = r \text{to} x = R.} \end{array}} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} \approx dA} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} = f^{\prime}(r)dr} \end{array}$$ where $$dr = R - r$$ . So we see that the area of the ring is approximately $$2\pi r(R - r)$$ square units. In words, the area of the ring is approximately equal to $${Circumference of the inner circle} \times {Thickness of the ring}$$

Applying the results of part (a) with $$r = 62,900$$ and $$dr = 50$$ , we find that the area of the ring is approximately $$2\pi(62,900)(50)$$ , or $$19,760,000$$ square kilometers, which is roughly $$4\%$$ of the earth’s surface.

section.paragraph: Before looking at the next example, we need to familiarize ourselves with some terminology. If a quantity with exact value $$q$$ is measured or calculated with an error of $$\Delta q$$ , then the quantity $$\Delta q \slash q$$ is called the relative error in the measurement or calculation of $$q$$ . If the quantity $$\Delta q \slash q$$ is expressed as a percentage, it is then called the percentage error. Because $$\Delta q$$ is approximated by $$dq$$ , we normally approximate the relative error $$\Delta q \slash q$$ by $$dq \slash q$$ .

list.item: If $$c$$ is a constant, then $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(c) =$$ $$0$$ . The Power Rule states that if $$n$$ is any real number, then $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x^{n}) =$$ $$nx^{n - 1}$$ . The Constant Multiple Rule states that if $$c$$ is a constant, then $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack cf(x)\rbrack =$$ $$cf^{\prime}(x)$$ . The Sum Rule states that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x) \pm g(x)\rbrack =$$ $$f^{\prime}(x) \pm g^{\prime}(x)$$ .

The Product Rule states that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x)g(x)\rbrack =$$ $$f(x)g^{\prime}(x) + g(x)f^{\prime}(x)$$ . The Quotient Rule states that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\lbrack f(x) \slash g(x)\rbrack =$$ $$\frac{g(x)f^{\prime}(x) - f(x)g^{\prime}(x)}{{\lbrack g(x)\rbrack}^{2}}$$ .

The Chain Rule states that if $$h(x) = g\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack$$ , then $$h^{\prime}(x) =$$ $$g^{\prime}\lbrack f(x)\rbrack f^{\prime}(x)$$ . The General Power Rule states that if $$h(x) = \left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n}$$ , then $$h^{\prime}(x) =$$ $$n{\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{n - 1}f^{\prime}(x)$$ .

If $$C$$ , $$R$$ , $$P$$ , and $$\overline{C}$$ denote the total cost function, the total revenue function, the profit function, and the average cost function, respectively, then $$C^{\prime}$$ denotes the marginal cost function, $$R^{\prime}$$ denotes the marginal revenue function, $$P^{\prime}$$ denotes the marginal profit function, and $$\overline{C}$$ denotes the marginal average cost function.

If $$f$$ is a differentiable demand function defined by $$x = f(p)$$ , then the elasticity of demand at price $$p$$ is given by $$E(p) =$$ $$- p\frac{f^{\prime}(p)}{f(p)}$$ . The demand is elastic if $$E(p) > 1$$ ; it is unitary if $$E(p) = 1$$ ; it is inelastic if $$E(p) < 1$$ .

Suppose a function $$y = f(x)$$ is defined implicitly by an equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$ . To find $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$ , we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $$x$$ and then solve the resulting equation for $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$ . The derivative of a term involving $$y$$ includes $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$ as a factor.

In a related-rates problem, we are given a relationship between $$x$$ and $$y$$ that depends on a third variable $$t$$ . Knowing the values of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}$$ at $$a$$ , we want to find $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}$$ at $$a$$ .

Let $$y = f(t)$$ and $$x = g(t)$$ . If $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ , then $$\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} =$$ $$\frac{- f(t)f^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)}$$ . If $$xy = 1$$ , then $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} =$$ $$\frac{- f(t)g^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)}$$ .

If a variable quantity $$x$$ changes from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ , then the increment in $$x$$ is $$\Delta x =$$ $$x_{2} - x_{1}$$ . If $$y = f(x)$$ and $$x$$ changes from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ , then the increment in $$y$$ is $$\Delta y =$$ $$f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)$$ .

If $$y = f(x)$$ , where $$f$$ is a differentiable function, then the differential $$\mathit{dx}$$ of $$x$$ is $$dx =$$ $$\Delta x$$ , where $$\Delta x$$ is an increment in $$x$$ , and the differential $$\mathit{dy}$$ of $$y$$ is $$dy =$$ $$f^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}$$ .
